source.title: The Potential Applications and Implications of Large Language Models in the Medical Field

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Figure 2 is referenced, but its plotted values are not included in the supplied text.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares medical-question accuracy across models of different stated sizes, bearing on downstream performance versus scale, but it does not measure held-out cross-entropy or fit scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own clinical-question accuracy results and qualitative comparisons across model sizes, relevant to V6. It does not test pretraining loss, power-law fits, extrapolation, or compute-optimal allocation; those versions are not tested.
record.test_reason: The study's own accuracy results on 22 clinical guideline questions are compared across four models of different sizes. This is a new, applied setting (retrieval-augmented medical QA) bearing loosely on V6. There is no controlled scale sweep, no loss measurement and no fit.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors say larger models tended to be more accurate, citing Kaplan, but stress that pretraining data quality and volume let LLaMA2 7B match a 13B model. They conclude LLMs on one high-end PC can support but not replace physicians.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates medical question-answering accuracy across existing models rather than measuring held-out loss or fitting scaling laws.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors note that model size and differences in base models and pretraining data affected results; LangChain retrieval sometimes failed to return relevant information.
record.problems: Only a few heterogeneous models are compared, with no controlled scaling sweep. Individual accuracy values and uncertainty estimates are not stated in the supplied prose, and the referenced figure's plotted values are unavailable here. ChatGPT's parameter count is presented as an estimate.
record.rows_left_out: Response-time comparisons were not extracted because they do not measure a claim version. Figure 2's numerical accuracy values could not be assigned from the supplied text.

untested.parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
Any fit or extrapolation from small runs.
Architecture shape at fixed parameter count.
Predictability in the sense of a fitted relationship between scale or loss and downstream accuracy, and any controlled within-family size sweep.

missing.what: Overall accuracy range across the four models, 27.3% to 72.7% (about 6/22 to 16/22 questions). The record wrongly says no accuracy numbers are stated.
Discussion statement that the smaller LLaMA2 7B often gave partial or superficial answers while WizardVicuna 13B gave more comprehensive ones. This qualifies R3.

record.verdict_notes: Very weak test: four heterogeneous models, 22 questions, a retrieval pipeline with inconsistent retrieval, and no uncertainty reported. The ChatGPT size is an estimate. Size is confounded with model family, pretraining data and online versus local deployment. Response time was correctly left out.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining cross-entropy and its scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
Fitting on small runs and predicting losses of substantially larger runs.
Loss-minimising parameter and token allocations under fixed compute budgets.
Controlled comparisons of architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Scaling-law behavior in other modalities or training regimes.
The study compares downstream accuracy across a few different models, but does not fit a predictive relationship, measure pretraining loss, or establish predictability across scales or tasks.
The study does not compare scaling-law fitting choices, exponents, or curve shapes.

rows.subject: WizardVicuna 13 B
rows.operation_detail: Answered key clinical questions derived from two guidelines; accuracy was evaluated.

conditions.value: 2018 antibiotic-use guideline for urinary tract infections and preliminary long-COVID recommendations

rows.baseline: KoVicuna 7 B; exact accuracy not stated
rows.value: Outperformed KoVicuna 7 B; exact accuracy not stated
rows.note: The prose gives the comparison but not the models' individual accuracy values.
rows.check: Exact per-model accuracies are only in Fig. 2. The text gives the overall range of 27.3%–72.7%. The comparison is cross-family (WizardVicuna vs KoVicuna), so it is not a controlled size contrast.

rows.subject: KoVicuna 7 B
rows.operation_detail: Answered key clinical questions derived from two guidelines; accuracy was evaluated.

conditions.value: 2018 antibiotic-use guideline for urinary tract infections and preliminary long-COVID recommendations

rows.baseline: WizardVicuna 13 B; exact accuracy not stated
rows.value: Was outperformed by WizardVicuna 13 B; exact accuracy not stated
rows.note: The study reports only the relative result in prose.
rows.check: Duplicates R1 from the other side. The smaller model losing to the larger one is what V6 predicts, so the state should be observed, not partial. Consider merging with R1.

rows.subject: LLaMA2 7 B
rows.stage_stated: pretrained and fine-tuned; fine-tuned using approximately one million prompts
rows.operation_detail: Answered key clinical questions derived from two guidelines; accuracy was evaluated.

conditions.value: 2018 antibiotic-use guideline for urinary tract infections and preliminary long-COVID recommendations

rows.baseline: WizardVicuna 13 B; exact accuracy not stated
rows.value: Accuracy described as comparable to WizardVicuna 13 B; exact accuracy not stated
rows.note: The authors attribute the comparison partly to differences in pretraining data and fine-tuning.
rows.check: LLaMA2 7B matched WizardVicuna 13B, so there is no size advantage in this pair; 'partial' understates this. The authors attribute the tie to more and better pretraining data. The Discussion also says LLaMA2 7B gave more superficial answers.

rows.subject: ChatGPT-3.5
rows.size_stated: estimated to contain over 1,750 B (1.75 trillion) parameters
rows.operation_detail: Answered key clinical questions derived from two guidelines; accuracy was evaluated.

conditions.value: 2018 antibiotic-use guideline for urinary tract infections and preliminary long-COVID recommendations

rows.baseline: The three offline models; individual accuracy values not stated
rows.value: Highest accuracy among the four models; exact accuracy not stated
rows.note: The paper also says ChatGPT had the shortest response time, which is not a measure named by V6.
rows.check: The ChatGPT-3.5 size of '1,750 B' is an unsourced estimate and likely off by 10x. ChatGPT also ran online under different compute, which confounds the size comparison. Its accuracy is presumably the 72.7% maximum.

relationships.condition: ChatGPT-3.5 vs the 7B/13B offline models; WizardVicuna 13B vs KoVicuna 7B
relationships.reason: The largest model had the highest accuracy and the 13B beat the 7B KoVicuna (R1, R2, R4). This is weak, uncontrolled cross-family evidence on 22 questions.
relationships.display_finding: The largest model achieved the highest accuracy, and WizardVicuna 13B outperformed KoVicuna 7B in an uncontrolled comparison across model families on 22 questions.

relationships.condition: LLaMA2 7B vs WizardVicuna 13B (different base model and pretraining data)
relationships.reason: The smaller LLaMA2 matched the 13B model, and the authors attribute this to pretraining data volume and quality rather than size (R3).
relationships.display_finding: The 7B model matched the 13B model, which the authors attributed to pretraining data volume and quality.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
